meta.titre: Redox Reactions: electron transfer, half-equations and electrolysis

sections.contenu_markdown: A mechanic in Douala leaves an iron bar in the rain, and a week later it is covered with brown rust. In a workshop nearby, a worker uses a battery to coat a bumper with shiny chrome. Both stories are about the same idea: electrons moving from one substance to another. Reactions in which electrons are transferred are called redox reactions, and they explain rusting, burning, batteries and the extraction of metals by electrolysis. Examiners often ask for half-equations at the electrodes, the identification of what is oxidised and reduced, and a simple calculation with current and time.

items: Atoms form positive ions by losing electrons and negative ions by gaining electrons.
An electric current in a molten or dissolved ionic compound is carried by moving ions.
A reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt.

sections.contenu_markdown:
A **redox reaction** is one in which oxidation and reduction happen together.

| | Oxidation | Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| Electrons | loss of electrons | gain of electrons |
| Oxygen | gain of oxygen | loss of oxygen |
| Hydrogen | loss of hydrogen | gain of hydrogen |

Memory aid: **OIL RIG** (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons).

- An **oxidising agent** takes electrons from another substance, so it is itself **reduced**.
- A **reducing agent** gives electrons, so it is itself **oxidised**.

Each redox equation can be split into two **half-equations**, which must balance in atoms and in charge:

$$\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}$$

$$\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$$

Adding them (the electrons cancel) gives the ionic equation $\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Cu}$. Zinc is oxidised (reducing agent) and copper(II) ions are reduced (oxidising agent).

**Electrolysis** is a redox process driven by electricity: at the **cathode** (negative electrode) positive ions gain electrons, which is reduction; at the **anode** (positive electrode) negative ions lose electrons, which is oxidation. Remember: **An Ox, Red Cat**.

variantes.nom: Tests for oxidising and reducing agents
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes a colour change.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) changes from **purple to colourless** when it is reduced, so the substance tested is a reducing agent. Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) changes from **orange to green** with a reducing agent. Potassium iodide solution turns **brown** with an oxidising agent because iodine forms: $\mathrm{Cl_{2}} + 2\mathrm{I^{-}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl^{-}} + \mathrm{I_{2}}$.

variantes.nom: Copper(II) sulphate solution: inert and copper electrodes
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the same solution is electrolysed with different electrodes.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Graphite (inert) electrodes.** Cathode: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$ (pink-brown copper deposits). Anode: $4\mathrm{OH^{-}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} + \mathrm{O_{2}} + 4\mathrm{e^{-}}$ (bubbles of oxygen). The blue colour fades because copper(II) ions are removed.

**Copper electrodes.** The cathode reaction is the same. At the anode the copper itself dissolves: $\mathrm{Cu} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}$. The anode gets smaller, the cathode gets bigger and the blue colour stays the same. This is used to purify copper: the impure copper is the anode and pure copper builds up on the cathode.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives a current and a time.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Charge $Q = I \times t$ (coulombs = amperes $\times$ seconds). One mole of electrons carries about $96\,500\ \mathrm{C}$ (use the value given in the question). Then $n(\text{electrons}) = Q / 96\,500$ and the amount of metal $= n(\text{electrons}) \div$ (charge on the ion). For example $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ needs 2 mol of electrons per mole of copper.

sections.enonce_markdown: A piece of zinc of mass 6.5 g is placed in an excess of blue copper(II) sulphate solution. (a) Write the two half-equations and the ionic equation. (b) Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. (c) State two observations. (d) Calculate the mass of copper formed, given that all the zinc reacts.

etapes.justification: Zinc is more reactive, so it loses electrons; copper(II) ions gain them.

etapes.action: Add them to get the ionic equation.
etapes.justification: The 2 electrons on each side cancel.
The oxidising agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidised.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Oxidising agent: copper(II) ions (copper(II) sulphate). Reducing agent: zinc.

etapes.justification: Colourless zinc ions replace blue copper ions, and copper metal forms.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The blue solution fades and a pink-brown solid (copper) forms on the zinc.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Zinc is oxidised and copper(II) ions are reduced; the blue colour fades and $6.4\ \mathrm{g}$ of copper is deposited.

items.pourquoi_faux: This reverses the definition. Oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL RIG).
items.correction_markdown: Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain of electrons.

items.erreur_markdown: "The oxidising agent is the substance that is oxidised."
items.pourquoi_faux: The oxidising agent causes oxidation of another substance by taking its electrons, so the agent itself is reduced.
items.correction_markdown: Oxidising agent = the substance reduced. Reducing agent = the substance oxidised.

items.pourquoi_faux: Reduction (gain of electrons) takes place at the cathode; the anode is where electrons are lost.
items.correction_markdown: Use An Ox, Red Cat: Anode = Oxidation, Reduction = Cathode.

items.pourquoi_faux: Electrons are gained at the cathode, so they must be on the left. This equation shows loss of electrons, which belongs to the anode when copper dissolves.

items.erreur_markdown: "A reaction is a redox reaction only if oxygen is involved."
items.pourquoi_faux: Oxygen is only one case. Any reaction with electron transfer is redox, for example displacement of metals or halogens.
items.correction_markdown: $\mathrm{Cl_{2}} + 2\mathrm{Br^{-}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl^{-}} + \mathrm{Br_{2}}$ is redox: bromide ions lose electrons and chlorine gains them.

items.enonce_markdown:
For each reaction, say which substance is oxidised, which is reduced and which is the oxidising agent.

(a) $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{H^{+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$

(b) $\mathrm{Cl_{2}} + 2\mathrm{Br^{-}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl^{-}} + \mathrm{Br_{2}}$

(c) $2\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{Cl_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 2\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Magnesium loses two electrons, so **Mg is oxidised**; hydrogen ions gain electrons, so $\mathrm{H^+}$ is reduced and is the **oxidising agent**.

(b) Bromide ions lose electrons, so **$\mathrm{Br^-}$ is oxidised**; chlorine gains electrons, so $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ is reduced and is the **oxidising agent**.

(c) Iron(II) ions become iron(III) by losing an electron each, so **$\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ is oxidised**; chlorine is reduced and is the **oxidising agent**.

items.enonce_markdown: Molten lead(II) bromide, $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}$, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. (a) Write the half-equation at each electrode and name the type of reaction at each. (b) State what is seen at each electrode. (c) Write the overall equation. (d) Why does solid lead(II) bromide not conduct?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Cathode (negative): $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb}$, **reduction**. Anode (positive): $2\mathrm{Br^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Br_{2}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}$, **oxidation**.

(b) At the cathode, silvery molten lead collects. At the anode, brown fumes of bromine are seen.

(c) $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb} + \mathrm{Br_{2}}$

(d) In the solid, the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, so no current is carried. In the molten state the ions are free to move.

items.enonce_markdown:
Copper is purified by electrolysis of copper(II) sulphate solution using an impure copper anode and a pure copper cathode. A current of 1.93 A passes for 5000 s. (Use: 1 mole of electrons carries $96\,500\ \mathrm{C}$.)

(a) Write the half-equation at each electrode. (b) Calculate the charge passed. (c) Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. (d) What happens to the mass of the anode and to the colour of the solution?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Anode: $\mathrm{Cu} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}$. Cathode: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$.

(b) $Q = I \times t = 1.93 \times 5000 = $ **$9\,650\ \mathrm{C}$**.

(c) $n(e^-) = \dfrac{9650}{96\,500} = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}$. Each $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ needs 2 electrons, so $n(\mathrm{Cu}) = \dfrac{0.100}{2} = 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $m = 0.0500 \times 64 = $ **3.2 g**.

(d) The anode **loses mass** because copper dissolves. The blue colour stays almost the same, because copper ions are added at the anode at the same rate as they are removed at the cathode.

items_markdown: Oxidation is loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen); reduction is gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen): OIL RIG.
An oxidising agent is reduced; a reducing agent is oxidised.
Half-equations must balance in atoms and in charge, with electrons on the left for reduction and on the right for oxidation.
In electrolysis, oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
With copper electrodes in copper(II) sulphate, the anode dissolves and copper is deposited on the cathode; with graphite, oxygen is released at the anode.
Charge $Q = It$; one mole of electrons carries about $96\,500\ \mathrm{C}$.
